influences/temples-to-churches/name: Temples turned into churches (Pantheon, Parthenon) and Gregory’s letter to Mellitus
influences/temples-to-churches/sourceCul: Pagan temples, shrines and festival customs of Rome, Greece, Egypt and Anglo-Saxon England
influences/temples-to-churches/christian: Former temples consecrated as churches, and Gregory the Great’s policy of reusing shrines and festivals for Christian worship
influences/temples-to-churches/evidenceN: The conversion of particular temples into churches is securely documented (the Pantheon in 609, the Parthenon probably in the late sixth century), and Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus of 601, preserved by Bede, explicitly advises adapting pagan shrines and festivals. What is overstated is the scale: temple conversions were relatively few and mostly late, often after buildings had stood empty for generations.
influences/temples-to-churches/popularCl: Christians systematically built their churches on top of pagan temples, so that Christian worship is pagan worship continued under new names (or, conversely, that Christians simply destroyed every temple).
influences/temples-to-churches/whatHisto: R. P. C. Hanson’s survey (1978) and later archaeology (Lavan and Mulryan, 2011) show that direct conversion of temples into churches was less common and later than often assumed: imperial laws closed temples from 391–392 and ordered their destruction or cleansing in 435 (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.25), but many buildings decayed or were quarried, some were violently destroyed (the Serapeum of Alexandria, 391/392), and only a minority became churches, mostly in the sixth and seventh centuries. The most famous cases are real and well documented. Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus is genuine evidence for a deliberate missionary strategy of adapting buildings and customs, though Gregory had written a month earlier urging King Æthelberht to destroy shrines, and archaeological evidence for reused shrines in England is thin. Reuse of sites and buildings expressed the victory of Christ over the gods; it did not mean the continuity of pagan worship.
influences/temples-to-churches/summary: Some famous pagan temples, including the Pantheon in Rome and the Parthenon in Athens, became churches, and in 601 Gregory the Great advised missionaries in England to purify and reuse pagan shrines and turn festivals into Christian feasts; such reuse was real but less widespread and later than popularly supposed.
influences/temples-to-churches/story:
In the fourth century Christian emperors moved gradually from tolerating to suppressing public pagan cult. Constantine stripped some temples of treasures; Theodosius I’s laws of 391–392 banned sacrifice and closed temples; and a law of 435 ordered surviving shrines to be destroyed and purified by the sign of the cross (Codex Theodosianus 16.10.25). Practice varied. In some cities bishops and monks destroyed temples: Marcellus of Apamea pulled down the temple of Zeus c. 386, Theophilus of Alexandria oversaw the destruction of the Serapeum in 391 or 392, and Martin of Tours demolished shrines in Gaul. The pagan orator Libanius protested to Theodosius (Oration 30, Pro templis) against monks who wrecked rural temples.

Conversion into churches was a different process, and generally later. R. P. C. Hanson’s survey found relatively few clear examples before the sixth century: Christians were often reluctant to worship in buildings they regarded as haunted by demons, and temple interiors were ill-suited to congregational worship. Notable conversions include the Temple of Isis at Philae (after c. 535–537), the Hephaisteion in Athens (as a church of St George) and the Temple of Athena at Syracuse, which became the cathedral, its columns still visible in the walls. The Parthenon was converted into a church of the Theotokos, probably in the late sixth century, and was the cathedral of Athens for centuries, a major pilgrimage site in Byzantine times according to Anthony Kaldellis.

The Pantheon in Rome is the classic case. According to the Liber Pontificalis, Pope Boniface IV obtained the disused temple from the emperor Phocas and dedicated it on 13 May 609 (or 610) as Santa Maria ad Martyres, translating martyrs’ relics into it. It is the main reason the building survives intact. In Rome, too, the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina became San Lorenzo in Miranda, and the Curia, the Senate house, became the church of Sant’Adriano in the seventh century.

The theory behind such reuse was articulated by Gregory the Great. Writing to Abbot Mellitus on 18 July 601, as he set out to join Augustine’s mission in Kent, Gregory revised his earlier advice to King Æthelberht to destroy shrines. The temples of the English, he wrote, should not be destroyed but cleansed of their idols, sprinkled with holy water and furnished with altars and relics, so that the people would come more readily to familiar places; and because they had been used to sacrificing oxen to demons, they should instead hold feasts in booths of branches on the days of dedication or of the martyrs, killing animals for food in praise of God. ‘It is impossible to cut off everything at once from hard hearts’, he explained, ‘for whoever wishes to climb to the highest place rises by steps, not by leaps’ (Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30). Augustine of Hippo had earlier allowed temples to be converted ‘to the worship of the true God’ (Letter 47.3), and his principle of ‘spoiling the Egyptians’ (On Christian Teaching 2.40.60) offered a wider rationale for taking over what was good in pagan culture.

How far Gregory’s policy was carried out is uncertain. Bede also records the high priest Coifi profaning and burning the temple at Goodmanham (2.13) and King Rædwald keeping a Christian altar and a pagan one in the same shrine (2.15), and archaeologists have found few clear Anglo-Saxon churches on pagan cult buildings. The letter has nonetheless become the classic text for both admirers of missionary adaptation and critics of Christian ‘paganisation’, from Conyers Middleton’s Letter from Rome (1729) onwards. Historians now treat it as evidence of a pragmatic, gradualist strategy in which reuse of place and custom signalled Christ’s victory over the old gods, rather than a wholesale continuation of pagan religion.
influences/temples-to-churches/howItHapp: Imperial laws of 391–392 and 435 closed temples and ordered their destruction or purification, leaving many buildings empty.
Some temples were destroyed by bishops, monks and crowds; others decayed or were quarried for materials.
From the sixth century prominent temples, often long disused, were consecrated as churches, usually with relics of martyrs.
Popes and emperors granted temple buildings to the church, as Phocas gave the Pantheon to Boniface IV.
Gregory the Great formulated a missionary policy of cleansing and reusing shrines and replacing sacrificial feasts with Christian festivals (601).
influences/temples-to-churches/examples/: The Pantheon, Rome, dedicated as Santa Maria ad Martyres by Boniface IV (609/610).
The Parthenon, Athens, converted to a church of the Theotokos (probably late sixth century), later a Latin cathedral (1204) and a mosque (after 1460).
The Temple of Athena, Syracuse, incorporated into the cathedral (seventh century).
The Temple of Isis at Philae, Egypt, partly converted into a church after its closure c. 535–537.
The Serapeum of Alexandria, destroyed in 391/392: the alternative fate.
Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus (601), preserved in Bede, Ecclesiastical History 1.30.
influences/temples-to-churches/defenders: Advised that English temples be cleansed and reused as churches and that sacrificial feasts become Christian festivals, rising ‘by steps, not by leaps’ (Letter to Mellitus, 601).
Allowed temples to be turned to the worship of the true God (Letter 47.3) and taught that Christians should take over pagan learning as Israel ‘spoiled the Egyptians’ (On Christian Teaching 2.40.60).
Preserved Gregory’s letters and presented the gradual Christianisation of English sacred places as a model of missionary wisdom (Ecclesiastical History, 731).
influences/temples-to-churches/critics/0: Pagan orator who protested to Theodosius I against monks destroying rural temples (Oration 30, c. 386).
influences/temples-to-churches/critics/1: Anglican clergyman whose A Letter from Rome (1729) argued that Roman Catholic worship was continuous with paganism, citing temples turned into churches.
influences/temples-to-churches/keptBy/0: Catholic Church, which still uses the Pantheon and other converted temples as churches.
influences/temples-to-churches/keptBy/1: Eastern Orthodox churches, which used converted temples in Greece and the Near East.
influences/temples-to-churches/keptBy/2: Catholic and Anglican missiology, which cites Gregory’s letter as a precedent for inculturation.
influences/temples-to-churches/rejectedB: Many Protestant polemicists since the Reformation, who saw such adaptation as the paganisation of the church.
Some early Christian zealots, who preferred to destroy temples rather than reuse them.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/sourceC: The everyday and official dress of the late Roman upper classes: tunic, paenula, dalmatic, scarf and napkin
influences/vestments-roman-dress/christi: Alb, chasuble, dalmatic, stole, maniple and pallium as distinctive clerical and liturgical vestments
influences/vestments-roman-dress/evidenc: The descent of the principal Western and Byzantine vestments from late Roman secular dress is the consensus of liturgical historians and is visible in mosaics such as San Vitale (547). The borrowing was of civilian and court clothing, not of pagan priestly dress, and the claim that the mitre derives from the fish-headdress of Dagon is a nineteenth-century myth.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/popular: Priests’ robes were copied from pagan priests — the mitre is the fish-hat of the god Dagon and the vestments are the costume of Babylonian or Roman pagan cults.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/whatHis: Christian clergy in the first centuries wore ordinary clothes. Pope Celestine I in 428 rebuked bishops in southern Gaul who had adopted a distinctive monastic cloak and girdle: ‘we should be distinguished from the people by our teaching, not our dress’. Vestments arose because the clergy kept the formal dress of late Roman gentlemen and officials while lay fashion moved on to the shorter tunics and trousers of the post-Roman world. By the sixth and seventh centuries this conservatism had turned ordinary garments into sacred ones. The alb is the tunica alba, the chasuble the travelling cloak (paenula or casula), the dalmatic a long-sleeved tunic named from Dalmatia, the maniple the ceremonial napkin (mappa), and the stole and pallium are probably derived from scarves and insignia of rank. The mitre appears only around the tenth and eleventh centuries, from Roman papal headgear (camelaucum), not from Mesopotamia; the Dagon theory goes back to Alexander Hislop’s The Two Babylons (1853) and has no historical basis.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/summary: The vestments of Catholic, Orthodox and many Anglican and Lutheran clergy are fossilised late Roman clothing. They became sacred when the clergy kept wearing them after everyone else had stopped.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/story:
The New Testament prescribes no clerical dress, and second- and third-century sources suggest that bishops and presbyters presided at the eucharist in their ordinary best clothes. The baptismal white garment and the image of the heavenly elders in white (Revelation 4:4) gave white clothing a symbolic charge, but there was no separate priestly wardrobe. When Pope Celestine I wrote to the bishops of the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne in 428, he criticised them for wearing the pallium and girdle of ascetics in church: clergy should stand out ‘by learning, not by clothing; by conduct, not by costume; by purity of mind, not by dress’.

The decisive change was the transformation of dress in the late Roman and post-Roman West. Long tunics and enveloping cloaks had been the formal dress of the Roman citizen and official; Germanic and military fashion brought in shorter tunics and trousers. The clergy, especially at the altar, kept the older dress, which gradually came to be regarded as sacred. The mosaics of San Vitale in Ravenna (547) show Archbishop Maximian in a chasuble-like cloak with the pallium, and his deacons in long tunics, standing beside Justinian’s court officials whose clothes are recognisably similar.

The individual garments can be traced. The alb (tunica alba or linea) was the basic undergarment of the Roman wardrobe; the chasuble (casula, ‘little house’) was the bell-shaped paenula worn by all classes for travel; the dalmatic was a wide-sleeved tunic that was once mocked as effeminate when worn by emperors and that the Liber Pontificalis, legendarily, says Pope Sylvester granted to Roman deacons. The maniple descends from the mappa, the napkin carried by Roman officials and used by consuls to start the games. The stole (orarium) and the pallium are more debated: probably scarves or insignia of honour. Their Byzantine equivalents — epitrachelion, omophorion, sakkos — developed alongside imperial court costume.

Meaning was added later. Medieval commentators such as Amalarius of Metz (ninth century) and Innocent III (De sacro altaris mysterio, c. 1195) gave each garment an allegorical sense — the chasuble as charity, the stole as the yoke of Christ — and Innocent III systematised the Roman sequence of liturgical colours. The mitre emerged in Rome in the tenth and eleventh centuries and spread to bishops by papal grant.

The Reformation divided over vestments. Lutherans kept many of them, especially in Scandinavia; in England the Vestiarian controversy began when John Hooper refused to be consecrated bishop in vestments (1550) and grew after Archbishop Parker’s Advertisements (1566) required the surplice. Reformed churches adopted the academic black gown, itself a late medieval university garment. In the twentieth century the Liturgical Movement revived ‘Gothic’ and simplified chasubles and the alb-and-stole spread to Methodist and other Protestant clergy, while some Protestant polemic — following Hislop — still claims a Babylonian origin that historians reject.
influences/vestments-roman-dress/howItHa: Early clergy wore ordinary formal Roman dress at worship; there was no special priestly costume.
From the fifth century lay fashion changed to shorter tunics and trousers, while clergy kept the older long garments.
By the sixth and seventh centuries these garments were reserved for liturgy and regarded as sacred.
Court insignia (pallium, napkin, scarves) were granted as marks of rank, especially by popes and emperors.
Medieval writers added allegorical meanings and Innocent III fixed a sequence of liturgical colours.

influences/vestments-roman-dress/defende: As Cardinal Lotario wrote De sacro altaris mysterio (c. 1195), interpreting each vestment and setting out the liturgical colours.
Accepted the surplice and some vestments as ‘things indifferent’ that the church may order for decency.
